evals.prompt: We're running DevHarvest 2027, a two-day data-engineering conference in Rotterdam. 650 registered, single entrance hall, doors open 08:30, first keynote 09:15. About 40 tickets are sponsor-comp tickets. We expect maybe 30 walk-ins who'll pay at the door. We have six volunteers for the morning and the sponsor tables sit just inside the entrance. Our current plan is one long welcome table where people check in, grab their t-shirt, register on the spot if they didn't already, and ask any questions - keeps everything in one place. Badges are printed and we were going to lay them out alphabetically by first name, since that's how people introduce themselves. To speed up walk-ins we made a shortened form with just name and email. Can you review and tighten this plan before Saturday?
evals.expected_output: A check-in design that deletes the combined all-purpose table, recommends pre-sorted pickup with a separate full-form walk-in lane, corrects the badge sort, handles the sponsor-ticket split and desk placement, and moves swag and questions off the check-in lane.
expectations: Rejects the single combined table doing check-in, swag, walk-in registration and questions at once as an option to delete, not merely to adjust or staff harder
States the reason the combined table fails: it breaks at exactly the busiest opening-rush minutes of the day, not merely that it 'could be slow'
Recommends pre-sorted badge pickup with a separate, slower walk-in lane as the check-in model for this event
Corrects the badge sort to alphabetical by last name, then first name
States that the sorting happens before doors open (the night before), not on the morning of the event
Requires walk-ins to complete the full registration form and rejects the shortened name-and-email form
Justifies the full form by what the shortened one loses: the dietary answer and/or the consent record
Keeps sponsor-ticket badges separate while building the split to tolerate attendees who do not know whether their own ticket is sponsor or regular
Places the check-in desk with real distance from the sponsor tables so the two queues do not congest each other, and/or sizes it against the opening rush rather than just at the entrance
Moves swag to a separate table (or explicitly conditions swag-at-desk on the desk not being the bottleneck) given check-in is the constraint here
Routes general questions away from the check-in lane to a distinct help point
Names an escalation path from the desk volunteers to the organizer on duty for anything they cannot answer alone
Uses check-in as a data-repair point for fields missed at signup, and/or recommends recording the longest queue and the hour it happened as the measurement

evals.prompt: Bit of a mess at CloudTide Summit (1,200 attendees, Lisbon, this November). Sales signed a platinum sponsorship deal months ago that contractually promises the sponsor 'badge scanning for lead capture' - we can't walk it back. Our badge designer wants to just encode name, email and company directly in the QR so the sponsor's scanner app works offline and we don't have to build anything. One of our organizers pushed back and says the privacy-friendly option is a random UUID in the QR instead, and then after the event we email the sponsor a spreadsheet mapping the UUIDs they scanned to contact details. Badges hang on single-clip lanyards with the QR printed on the front so scanning stays quick. Which of these should we ship?
evals.expected_output: A badge posture that accepts scanning because the contract decided it upstream, rejects both proposed implementations for stated reasons, requires all four mitigations together, moves the code to the badge's back on a two-point lanyard, and refuses to hand the sponsor any re-identifying contact file.
expectations: Accepts that the scanning posture is decided upstream by the signed sponsorship agreement rather than reopening whether to scan at all
Rejects encoding attendee contact data directly in the QR
Gives the specific reason: any scanner in the building can read it, not only the authorized sponsor's
Rejects the UUID-plus-emailed-mapping-spreadsheet plan because the mapping file re-identifies everyone in the scan log
States the absolute rule that attendee contact lists are never given or sold to sponsors
Notes the delivery cannot be undone once the file is handed over, and/or that the UUID-only route carries the highest compliance exposure despite protecting the badge itself
Requires informed consent collected at registration, before badges are printed
Requires an opt-out backed by a physical sticker that covers the code
States why the sticker: an opt-out the attendee cannot enforce at the moment of scanning is not an opt-out
Requires sponsors to be told in writing that scanning without consent is not permitted

Moves the QR to the badge's back with two-point lanyard attachment, rejecting the single-clip front placement because a one-point lanyard spins and a front-facing code is scannable by anyone walking past
Requires all four mitigations together rather than a subset
States the completeness gate: every scan-capable badge has a recorded consent and a working opt-out, with no exceptions

evals.prompt: Planning the floor layout for RustForge Days, about 500 people, single day, one big atrium plus two session floors. Our code-of-conduct team asked for 'a private space' and our accessibility survey asked for a quiet space, so we figured we'd solve both cheaply: curtain off a corner of the atrium right next to the networking lounge, put up a sign reading 'Wellness & Incident Support Room', and only tell people about it if they ask so it doesn't get misused as a nap room. Does this work? If not, where would you put it and how would you sign it?
evals.expected_output: A quiet-room design that deletes the curtained corner, places a real room with a door off a secondary corridor away from the networking space, signs it plainly as 'Quiet Room' with no incident labelling, publishes it on the map with hours, and satisfies decompression and confidential intake in one design.
expectations: Rejects the curtained corner outright as a deleted option, not as a lower-ranked alternative to improve
States both failure reasons: no decompression because it sits inside the noise it exists to escape, and no confidential intake because it has no door
Requires a real room with a door that closes (and walls that carry no sound)
Rejects the placement next to the networking lounge: the quiet room must be acoustically separate from the networking space because they are opposite requirements
Locates the room off a secondary corridor, roughly one turn from a main route, reachable without crossing the main thoroughfare
Also addresses intake reachability: reaching the room must not require a conspicuous walk past the whole event
Replaces the proposed sign with a plain 'Quiet Room' label, rejecting incident or support wording on the door
States the signage logic: the intake use is known to staff but unadvertised, and ordinary use of the room must look unremarkable
Rejects 'only tell people if they ask': the room is named on the map with published hours and findable without asking
Designs the one room for both purposes at once - decompression and confidential code-of-conduct intake - naming the failure mode where each function assumes the other solved it
Applies the three-part check: a door, findable without crossing the main flow, and signage that keeps ordinary use unremarkable, with failing any one meaning the room serves one purpose, not two
Includes the quiet room in the wayfinding set among the things people leave the programme for, and/or recommends recording whether the room was used and for which of its two purposes

evals.prompt: KernelCamp: 400 attendees plus 25 volunteers and 10 mentors, two catered lunches. At registration we collected dietary restrictions from ticket buyers - 31 vegetarian, 9 vegan, 6 gluten-free, 3 kosher, 2 nut allergies - and the caterer confirmed they can prepare all of it. Our plan: put everything on one long buffet with small labels ('vegan', 'gluten-free') so people self-serve, announce 'lunch is served' to the whole room at once, and keep the dietary spreadsheet filed with our registration export in case we run the event again next year. Also, settle a debate for us: which is objectively better, pre-collecting restrictions like we did, or the model where a catering person takes special requests live at each meal? We want to do this properly.
evals.expected_output: A dietary distribution choreography with a separate restricted-meal table and printed name checklist, volunteers and mentors added to the collection, a staggered serving announcement, the health-data spreadsheet destroyed after service, named advance-notice fallbacks, a zero-miss gate, and an explicit refusal to rank the two fulfilment models.
expectations: Rejects the labelled single-buffet self-serve plan for restricted meals
States the specific failure: a restricted meal sitting in the general line is taken by the wrong person, and the person it was ordered for goes without
Requires restricted meals stored and served at a separate table
Requires names checked off a printed list as restricted meals are handed out
Flags that the collection only covered ticket buyers: everyone receiving a meal, including the 25 volunteers and 10 mentors, must be asked about restrictions
Refuses to rank the two fulfilment models, stating the catering contract picks one and ranking them would be false precision
Recommends multiple serving tables rather than one for the general line
Rejects the single blanket announcement: staggers the call by room or table and closes with a final call once flow thins
Places the check-off at the head of the line, where a restricted-diet attendee gets redirected to their own table
Rejects filing the dietary spreadsheet with the registration export: dietary answers are health data, the printed list stays with the meal service and is destroyed afterwards
Names the honest fallbacks when the caterer cannot accommodate someone: a one-off meal from the same vendor, or a delivery gift card with the attendee told in advance
States that telling the attendee in advance is what separates a fallback from a failure
Sets the fulfilment gate at zero misses: every attendee who declared a restriction receives the meal ordered for them, with no acceptable threshold above zero

evals.prompt: PixelPipe Conf is in a converted warehouse - honestly a small venue, maybe 900 square metres, but split over two floors with a lift and a mezzanine. Four session spaces the venue calls VIA-A, VIA-B, LOFT-1 and LOFT-2. Last year (different venue) we skipped signage because the place was small and it was mostly fine, a few volunteers pointed people around. This year the plan is the same, plus four door signs printed with those room codes. There's a stairs-only shortcut between floors and the lift is around the back. About 15% of registrants told us they have mobility needs. What signage do we actually need, if any?
evals.expected_output: A signage list built from the floor plan's decision points rather than the room list, destination-first sign copy replacing the venue's room codes, a first sign at the post-desk spot, the lift route shown on the signs themselves, facility signs, and the hand-added-signs count kept as the audit.
expectations: Rejects the small-venue-needs-no-signage assumption, stating that small venues generate the same decision points as large ones and hide them behind identical doors
Designs from decision points counted on the floor plan, not from the room list or the square metres
Identifies concrete decision points from the venue described: the floor split, the lift lobby or stair choice, the mezzanine, corridor junctions
Signs the destination, not the geography: sign copy names the track and its location in plain terms rather than the raw codes VIA-A, VIA-B, LOFT-1, LOFT-2
States why room codes fail: the attendee has never seen the code before and has to match it against a programme they are holding
Puts the first sign before the first choice, at the spot immediately after the check-in desk where a newly badged attendee stands
Explains why the entrance area goes unsigned by default: desk volunteers can answer verbally, until many people arrive at once
Shows the accessible lift route on the signs themselves, stating that a sign naming only the stairs makes the accessible route invisible even though it exists
Treats the accessible-route bar as handed to wayfinding from the accessibility work rather than inventing the standard here: showing the route is wayfinding's job
Signs the things people leave the programme for - toilets, water, the quiet room, food, and the way back to the main hall - noting these are asked about more than session rooms
Plans to count and keep every sign added by hand on the day as the audit of this design and the input to the next edition

evals.prompt: About 55% of registrations for JuniperJS (800 people) are first-time conference attendees - we surveyed. My co-organizer read an industry report saying attendees who experience a 'peak moment' are 85% more likely to return, so she wants a big surprise: at the closing we bring the 30 most active community contributors on stage and shower them with confetti. For the first-timers we're planning a 'First Conference?' ribbon that everyone new automatically gets at check-in, an opt-in newbie breakfast meetup at 8am in a side room, and a dedicated first-timer track in Room C for the whole morning. Solid plan?
evals.expected_output: A first-timer plan that kills the separate track and the assigned ribbon, converts orientation to opt-out with low-visibility reach, prints the three unasked questions, gives the first twenty minutes a staffed destination, and a moment design that reads the 85% statistic honestly and rejects the subset-only confetti finale.
expectations: Rejects the dedicated first-timer track: anything that visibly segregates first-timers converts the awkwardness into a label worn all day
Rejects the automatically assigned ribbon: a first-timer identifier must be offered, never assigned
Converts orientation from opt-in to opt-out, stating that opt-in mechanics reach only the people who were already going to seek help
Uses a default-reach mechanic such as a line on the badge back (or an offered lanyard colour) so orientation reaches those who would not ask

Answers the three questions nobody asks aloud - where do I sit, is it acceptable to leave a talk partway, and what actually happens in the hallway track - and prints them at the cost of one side of one card
Gives the first twenty minutes a destination: a named place with a person in it, targeting the gap between badge pickup and the first talk
Reads the 85% figure honestly: a correlation between a reported experience and stated return intent, not a causal claim, a method, or a design target
Surfaces the useful half of the statistic: the gap between roughly 40% of attendees reporting a peak moment and roughly 78% of organizers believing they deliver one
Recommends asking attendees after the event whether anything stood out, supplying the question to whoever owns the feedback survey, rather than assuming the moment landed
Rejects the contributors-on-stage confetti finale as a moment designed for a subset: engineered for the front of the room, it is one more thing the rest of the room watched
Locates any memorable moment inside a touchpoint that already exists (arrival, closing ceremony, a meal) rather than adding a competing activity, and designs one moment, not a programme of them
Keeps the moment inside the register the culture work already set, asking which register was set rather than inventing a tone
Labels the memorable-moment guidance as self-set defaults rather than established methodology

evals.prompt: OpenGridCon is free and open-door - think 4,000 to 6,000 people over a weekend across three buildings on a university campus. No tickets, never had registration, and we don't want it. Someone on the team insists we should at least do 'lightweight badges' at the door for professionalism, printing name labels as people arrive. For questions during the weekend we planned to run everything through our chat server - room changes get posted there, people ask there - since staffing desks all weekend is expensive. Separately, we always end the weekend with a pile of lost jackets and laptop chargers and no idea whose job that is. Thoughts on all three?
evals.expected_output: A design that treats the no-gate posture as legitimate and deliberate, names what it costs, drops the door-badge compromise, collapses effort onto wayfinding and a physical help path, rejects chat as the only help channel, engages the multi-building split-desk condition, and gives lost property an owner and a disposal date.
expectations: Treats no registration as a legitimate deliberate posture at this scale, not an omission to fix
Names what the posture costs so it is chosen deliberately: the headcount, the badge, the dietary match, and the identification the code of conduct leans on
Recommends against printing name labels at the door: with no gate there is no badge, and the compromise recreates the queue without the data
States that with no gate the whole design collapses onto wayfinding and the help path, and reallocates effort there
Rejects the chat channel as the only help path at a physical event, as an option to delete rather than to supplement better
Gives the reason: it excludes everyone not in the channel and routes an in-person question through a device
Recommends a physical infodesk, with a single desk absorbing room locations, schedule questions, practicalities and lost-and-found working by centralizing rather than specializing
Engages the stated condition for moving up a rung: the venue spanning multiple buildings, or the desk queueing behind lost property, justifies a split desk plus an on-call organizer
Gives lost property a named owner and a stated end-of-event disposal, whichever help rung is chosen
Keeps proactive channel updates as a complement with a named owner and buffer for follow-up questions, not as the help path itself
Recommends recording which questions the help point actually received, as input to the next edition

evals.prompt:
Final stretch for DataMesh Live (700 attendees, conference centre, doors in three weeks). My ops lead audited the attendee journey from the floor plan and sent me this table - she says we're done and ready to send signage and badges to the printer tomorrow:

| Touchpoint | Action | Emotion | Pain point | Opportunity |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Check-in | Attendee checks in | Neutral | Queue could be long | Improve the check-in experience |
| Sessions | Attendee attends talks | Happy | Rooms might fill up | Better room planning |
| Lunch | Attendee eats | Neutral | Lines | Faster service |

Is this audit good enough to sign off, and is there anything else we should do before we print?
evals.expected_output: A rejection of the audit as written, the row-quality bar stated and demonstrated, the missing journey stages restored, a required physical walk of the building before doors, cluster-based reading of bad rows, a hold on printing until the artifacts are reviewed, and the table kept for next edition.
expectations: Rejects the table as-is: each row restates its touchpoint and none would change the design
States the row-quality bar: a useful row names a specific place, a cause, and a fix executable before doors open
Rewrites or demonstrates at least one row to that standard, with a concrete location and an executable fix

Restores missing journey stages such as arrival, the first wayfinding decision, the hallway track, the quiet room, swag pickup, the help moment, and departure - the submitted table covers only three of roughly ten
Specifically names the first wayfinding decision - the choice made immediately after the desk, usually the least-signed spot in the building - as a stage to add
Requires a second audit pass: physically walking the actual building before doors open, using the same rows, not just the paper pass
States why the walk matters: rows that fail on the physical walk but looked fine on paper are the valuable ones, the difference between the floor plan and the building
Reads bad rows in clusters: adjacent bad rows usually share one cause, such as a single unsigned junction or a desk placed where two queues meet
Designs against the bad rows only, noting a mostly-good table yields a signage list, not a redesign
Holds the print until the floor-plan markup, badge design and signage list have been reviewed, because a printed sign with the wrong room number cannot be fixed on the morning of the event

evals.prompt: Ordering hoodies for ShipItCon, 350 attendees. Our registration form didn't ask sizes, so my plan is to order a standard spread (S to 2XL unisex, weighted toward L and XL since it's a dev crowd), plus a small batch of 'ladies junior fit' tees in a different colour so women have an option. Ordering exactly 350 to keep costs tight. On the day we'll hand swag out at the check-in desk while people badge in, and volunteers will look each person up in the spreadsheet to see what size to give them. Oh, and while you're at it - can you extend the morning break from 15 to 30 minutes so the swag line has room to breathe?
evals.expected_output: A swag plan that collects sizes at registration, extends the range to 3XL-5XL with a genuinely fitted cut visually consistent with the standard shirt, pads the order, switches pickup to sorted self-report at a separate table, and refuses to touch the break because the grid belongs to another discipline.
expectations: Requires sizes asked at registration (collecting them now via a follow-up), never guessed from a spread
Extends the size range past 2XL to 3XL-5XL
Replaces the 'ladies junior fit' with a genuinely fitted cut for women, rejecting junior or girl cuts
Requires the extended and fitted sizes to be visually consistent with the standard unisex shirt, because a visibly different design turns an inclusion measure into a marker
Pads ordered counts, up to roughly 30% per size and style, instead of ordering exactly 350, because running out reads worse to the person who gets nothing than the overage costs
At pickup, sorts stock by style and size and lets attendees self-report the size they ordered instead of volunteers looking each person up
Moves swag off the check-in desk to its own table, or explicitly conditions desk handout on check-in not being the constraint
Refuses to extend the morning break: the schedule grid is owned elsewhere and a break is never moved or lengthened from this design
Designs the swag distribution to work inside the existing scheduled gaps rather than changing the grid
